title: Good Influence at Scale
subtitle: Help others succeed beyond your immediate team
summary: Pip’s redesign proposal lands badly. Without authority, influence depends on trust, evidence, relationships, and understanding other people’s needs. Listening, teaching, writing, and connecting teams let good judgment travel through the workshop without requiring Pip to own every outcome.

concepts.title: Influence
concepts.body: Pip arrives with a redesign; the owning team wanted help understanding a support report. Influence works through trust, evidence, and relationships when formal authority is absent. Pip asks what the team is trying to achieve and whether advice would help before prescribing a solution. Seniority does not make the recommendation right. Relevant context makes a design note usable; rank alone cannot supply it.

steps.text: Pip asks whether advice would be useful.
A technically sound proposal may miss the request.
Trust and evidence make a recommendation usable.

concepts.title: Stakeholders
concepts.body: Support sees customer frustration; engineering sees a fragile dependency; product sees an interrupted journey. Pip listens for the constraints behind each position instead of treating disagreement as ignorance. Stakeholders experience different consequences and hold information a workable decision needs. Their goals may all be legitimate. The workshop needs an intervention people can sustain, not a winner in a contest over whose perspective counts.

steps.text: Pip asks who experiences the consequences.
Support sees the customer’s recurring pain.
Find a workable intervention across those perspectives.

concepts.title: Teaching
concepts.body: The same review question reaches Pip from three teams. Instead of answering privately forever, Pip organizes a shared practice session with examples and room for questions. Teaching scales judgment when colleagues can apply it later without the teacher present. A guide or workshop should build that independence. Repeating the answer to a larger audience is not enough if nobody gets to try the reasoning.

steps.text: Pip notices the same question arriving repeatedly.
Private answers keep the dependency alive.
Help teams apply the judgment without Pip present.

concepts.title: Bridge
concepts.body: A customer describes a confusing failure; the owning team discusses API contracts. Pip translates the missing context and brings the people together. A bridge preserves important meaning on both sides, connecting complementary knowledge. Sometimes removing an obstacle or enabling a conversation is the most valuable contribution. Pip can act as a catalyst without owning the eventual project—or collecting its credit.

steps.text: Pip connects people with complementary knowledge.
The owning team can act without Pip claiming the whole outcome.

misconceptions.claim: a staff-plus role is mainly about applying a universal formula.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter treats judgment as contextual: identify forces, listen to evidence, and adapt the response to the actual system and people.

misconceptions.claim: A visible activity or artifact proves the work is complete.
misconceptions.correction: Completion requires a useful outcome, shared understanding, and a way to notice whether the decision worked over time.

scenario.title: Build influence
scenario.context: Support brings Pip recurring customer pain. The owning workshop team distrusts architecture proposals, and Pip cannot mandate a redesign.

options.label: Listen and bridge
options.benefit: Customer examples and team constraints shape a shared experiment.
options.cost: Listening may overturn Pip’s preferred technical solution.
options.consequence: Pip invites support and the owners into the diagnosis. Together they choose a small experiment with a clear purpose.

options.label: Publish a mandate
options.benefit: A redesign is quick to announce.
options.cost: An unsupported mandate spends trust and invites resistance.
options.consequence: The proposal lacks ownership. The team routes around it, even if some technical ideas were sound.

scenario.debrief: Influence begins with understanding the problem other people have. Pip earns a useful role in the conversation rather than assuming one.

quiz.question: Before giving unsolicited advice, what is a useful first step?
options: Ask what the person needs and whether advice would help
Explain why their approach is wrong
quiz.explanation: Understanding the need and obtaining an opening makes advice more useful.

quiz.question: The same question repeatedly reaches you from different teams. What may scale your help?
options: A shared teaching session with practice and examples
Requiring your approval for the task
quiz.explanation: Teaching can help many people apply the idea independently.

quiz.question: What does acting as a catalyst emphasize?
options: Receiving visible credit for every improvement
Connecting people or removing obstacles so useful work can happen
quiz.explanation: Influence can enable an outcome without retaining ownership of it.

exercise.title: Make the next move legible
exercise.prompt: Describe a staff-level decision, the people and terrain involved, and the route by which you will learn whether it worked.

fields.label: Who has missing context?
fields.placeholder: Write the concrete facts, people, and constraint.

fields.label: What would listening change?
fields.placeholder: State the choice and its trade-off.

fields.label: How can the group own the experiment?
fields.placeholder: Name the evidence or conversation that will revisit it.
